01


**TL;DR**


- KYB verification turnaround time by risk tier splits into automated, manual-review and enhanced due diligence paths.
- Low-risk cases clear on automated checks; high-risk cases wait on people and documents.
- Track median and 90th-percentile time per tier, not one blended average.
- Infinite builds compliance screening into account opening, so KYB is one step, not a separate project.


02


## Why this matters


A single average KYB time hides the problem. One slow high-risk case and a hundred instant low-risk cases blend into a number that describes neither. Founders quote the blend, then wonder why onboarding feels slow.


Tiering fixes that. Each tier has a different bottleneck, so each needs a different target. For a plain-language baseline on the overall process, see[how long KYB verification takes](https://infinite.net/learn/insights/how-long-does-kyb-verification-take) .


03


## The short answer


**There is no honest universal number.** Published turnaround figures vary by vendor, jurisdiction, entity type and how complete the applicant's documents are, and no neutral public dataset breaks them out by risk tier. Any single figure quoted without scope is marketing.


What holds across providers is the ordering: low-risk cases finish fastest, standard cases take longer, and high-risk cases take the longest. The rest of this page explains why, so you can set targets against your own data.


04

This table ranks tiers by the work involved. It carries no invented durations. Fill the last column from your own case logs.

- What drives the time: Registry lookup speed, clean ownership data

**The slowest tier is the one with the most human steps.** Low-risk entities lead on speed; high-risk entities trail, because enhanced due diligence is a review process, not a lookup.


05


## What sits in each tier


### Low risk


A domestic operating company with a clean registry record, a short ownership chain and no adverse screening hits. The checks are mostly automated: business registry match, sanctions and watchlist screening, beneficial owner identification.


The usual delay is not the check. It is the applicant uploading the wrong document or a mismatched legal name.


### Medium risk


Cases with more than one ownership layer, a foreign registration, or a partial data match. An analyst reviews what automation could not settle.


The US Customer Due Diligence rule from FinCEN sets the reference points here: identify each individual owning 25 percent or more of a legal entity, plus one individual with significant control. Every extra layer between the applicant and those people adds review time.


### High risk


High-risk triggers include complex or opaque ownership, higher-risk jurisdictions, cash-intensive or crypto-adjacent activity, and politically exposed owners. The Financial Action Task Force's risk-based approach expects enhanced due diligence for these cases: more evidence, deeper checks, and senior approval.


Shell-like structures are the sharpest example. Our guide on[how KYB works for shell companies](https://infinite.net/learn/insights/how-does-kyb-verification-work-for-shell-companies) covers what reviewers look for and why these cases stall.


06


## High and low commentary


Low-risk cases lead on speed because nothing requires a person. High-risk cases trail because each open question, such as the origin of funds or an unnamed owner, restarts a document request cycle with the applicant.


The gap inside a tier is often wider than the gap between tiers. A medium-risk case with complete documents can finish before a low-risk case waiting on a corrected certificate. That is why the 90th percentile matters more than the median.


07


## Methodology and limits


The tier structure above reflects the risk-based approach in FATF guidance and the beneficial ownership requirements in FinCEN's CDD rule, both public. Turnaround figures are deliberately left for you to fill, because no source we can cite publishes tier-level durations with a stated scope and period.


**Named limitation:** tier definitions differ between institutions. One bank's medium is another's high, so compare your numbers against your own history first and against vendors second.


08


## How to use these benchmarks


- **Log every case with its tier and three timestamps:** submitted, documents complete, decision. Time spent waiting on the applicant is not verification time.
- **Report median and 90th percentile per tier.** Set the target on the 90th percentile; that is the case your customer remembers.
- **Split vendor time from applicant time.** If most delay is the applicant, faster software will not fix it. Better document checklists will.
- **Route by tier at intake.** Sending low-risk cases down the automated path and reserving analysts for the rest protects both speed and quality.


Tiering also decides which providers fit. For a vendor-by-vendor view, see[KYB software ranked by turnaround time](https://infinite.net/learn/insights/kyb-verification-software-ranked-by-turnaround-time) .


09


## Where high-risk businesses fit


High-risk does not mean declined. It means more evidence and a longer queue. Businesses in higher-risk sectors can still get compliant banking when they arrive with documents ready; the details are in our guide on[compliant banking for high-risk businesses](https://infinite.net/learn/insights/can-high-risk-businesses-get-compliant-banking) .

## FAQ


**What is KYB verification turnaround time by risk tier?**


It is the time from a complete application to a KYB decision, measured separately for low, medium and high-risk entities. Tiers differ because higher risk adds manual review and enhanced due diligence.


**Which risk tier takes the longest to verify?**


High-risk cases take the longest. They require enhanced due diligence, such as source-of-funds evidence and senior approval, which depends on people and applicant responses.


**Is there a standard industry benchmark for KYB turnaround?**


No neutral public benchmark breaks KYB turnaround out by tier. Vendor figures differ in scope, so build your own benchmark from case logs.


**Why is the 90th percentile better than the average?**


The average hides slow outliers. The 90th percentile shows the wait your slowest customers experience, which is what drives complaints and drop-off.


**What slows down a low-risk KYB case?**


Applicant errors, mainly. Wrong documents, mismatched legal names and missing ownership details cause most delays in otherwise clean cases.


**Who counts as a beneficial owner in the US?**


Under FinCEN's CDD rule, each individual who owns 25 percent or more of a legal entity, plus one individual with significant control over it.


**Can automation speed up high-risk KYB?**


It speeds up the data collection and screening steps. The final judgment on source of funds and ownership still needs a reviewer.


12


## One last thing


The cheapest way to cut turnaround in 2026 is to fix intake, not the review. A document checklist sent before the application, tied to the entity type, removes the restart cycles that dominate medium and high-risk cases. Measure applicant wait time separately for a month and you will see where the days go.
